strengths: Significant theoretical improvements: 200× tighter bias bounds than prior work (Theorem 1) with independence from n; adaptive convergence rates showing O(1/m) for well-separated classes
Novel problem formulation: Identifies and formalizes estimation with corrupted soft labels, a practically relevant scenario from distribution shifts and LLM bias
Strong theoretical framework for corrupted labels: Theorem 2 elegantly shows only order preservation is needed (weaker than exact values); sophisticated application of isotonic regression theory
Adaptive convergence analysis: LErr function provides interpretable understanding of how bias decay depends on class separation and label proximity to decision boundary
Comprehensive experimental validation: Synthetic experiments validate theory, real-world experiments on CIFAR-10H/Fashion-MNIST-H, extensive corruption parameter ablations (Section D.1)
Practical instance-free property: Methods don't require input instances, enabling applications in privacy-sensitive scenarios like medical diagnosis
Clear motivation and presentation: Well-articulated problem with concrete examples; good use of figures to illustrate concepts and results
weaknesses: Severe scope limitation: Restriction to binary classification substantially limits applicability; multi-class extension only mentioned as future work, excluding many modern applications

Restrictive assumptions in corrupted setting: (1) Theorem 2 assumes η̃ᵢ=f(ηᵢ) with f strictly increasing—deterministic relationship may not hold with random human/LLM corruption; (2) Theorem 3 requires f'(η)≥c>0, excluding flat functions; theoretical gap acknowledged but unresolved
Missing assumption verification on real data: No verification that CIFAR-10H soft labels satisfy the increasing function assumption; paper doesn't validate whether corruption model holds in practice
Slower convergence rate unexplained: n^(-1/3) term in Theorem 2 is slower than typical statistical rates; no discussion of whether this is fundamental or an artifact of the proof technique
Unknown constants limit practical implications: Constants C and C' in Theorems 2-3 are unspecified; finite-sample performance could depend critically on these constants

Additional data requirements not well justified: Section 3 requires hard labels {yᵢ} for calibration, unlike earlier methods. Advantage over directly averaging hard labels (Section 2) is unclear; practical guidance on when to use each approach is missing

Limited experimental comparisons: (1) Only Ishida et al. (2023) compared for Bayes error estimation; other methods (Theisen et al. 2021, Noshad et al. 2019) not empirically compared; (2) Calibration baselines limited to histogram binning and beta calibration; modern methods like temperature scaling omitted; (3) Only two real datasets (CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST-H); more diverse datasets needed

Incomplete robustness analysis: Section D.2 shows isotonic calibration is empirically robust to small derivatives, but this is relegated to appendix and lacks theoretical explanation; no guidance on robustness to ordering assumption violations

Gap between theory and practice: All results are asymptotic; finite-sample behavior with typical dataset sizes not thoroughly discussed; computable bound (Corollary 2) requires accurate upper bound on Err* but sensitivity to this input is unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with compelling CIFAR-10H example demonstrating corrupted soft labels in real datasets
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 1 provides tighter n-independent bounds (>200× improvement in practical settings) that adapt to class separation via the LErr function
Important negative result (Example 2) clearly showing perfect calibration is insufficient, motivating the need for calibration-aware Bayes error estimation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets (vision, NLP, peer-review) with FeeBee framework for assessing methods without ground truth
Consistent empirical finding that isotonic calibration outperforms alternatives across all datasets (Table 1), providing actionable practical insight
Instance-free approach is valuable for privacy-sensitive applications where input instances are unavailable
Thorough supplementary material with complete proofs, ablations on corruption functions, and analysis of order breakage
weaknesses: Restrictive assumptions for main contribution (Section 3): Theorem 2 requires order-preserving corruptions η̃ᵢ = f(ηᵢ), which is unverifiable in practice and violated in realistic scenarios (Appendix D.5 shows performance degradation with order breakage, but no theory provided)

Theory-practice gap: While isotonic calibration provably works under order preservation, empirical success when assumptions are violated (D.2.2, D.5) lacks theoretical explanation. Beta calibration fails even when 'well-specified,' remaining unexplained
Limited scope to binary classification significantly restricts applicability; extension to multi-class is mentioned only as future work despite being essential for real-world impact
Section 2's improvement over Ishida et al. (2023) is solid but somewhat incremental, using standard techniques (Jensen's inequality, plug-in estimation) without substantial conceptual novelty

Weak explanation for why isotonic calibration specifically works: Paper shows empirically it's best but provides limited insight into the mechanisms beyond invoking shape-constrained regression theory
Practical guidance insufficient: No method provided to verify order-preservation assumption in real data; no guidance on when practitioners should trust the method or when it may fail
Experimental comparisons limited to calibration methods; missing comparisons to recent alternative Bayes error estimators reviewed in Appendix A (e.g., density-based or normalizing flow approaches)
